extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners preparing/responding to office actions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether patent claims satisfy 35 U.S.C. §101 subject matter eligibility, using the MPEP workflow (Step 1 statutory categories; Step 2 Alice/Mayo two-part test) and related doctrines. Intended to direct examiners how to interpret claims (BRI), identify judicial exceptions, apply the two-part test, and formulate or support rejections or allowances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two criteria for subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: First, the claimed invention must be to one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter). Second, the claimed invention must qualify as patent-eligible subject matter, i.e., the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judicial exceptions are abstract ideas, laws of nature and natural phenomena (including products of nature). Use the Alice/Mayo two-part test to analyze judicial exceptions. The manual emphasizes that the two-part Alice/Mayo test is the only test that should be used to evaluate eligibility under examination; other tests (e.g., machine-or-transformation) are useful as clues but not as standalone tests. See MPEP §§ 2106.03, 2106.04, and 2106.05 for detailed guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim as a whole before eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim must be established prior to examining a claim for eligibility because BRI sets the boundaries of the coverage sought by the claim and influences whether the claim seeks to cover subject matter beyond the statutory categories or encompasses judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI affects both Step 1 (statutory category) and Step 2 (Alice/Mayo analysis). Examiners should construe the claim in light of the entire disclosure and apply BRI consistently (examples: Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish). If BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1. See MPEP § 2111 for more on claim interpretation and examples in the text (e.g., carrier waves in machine-readable medium claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1 — Claim falls within one of the four statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim as a whole is to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (35 U.S.C. 101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Processes are acts or series of acts (methods). Machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter generally must have physical or tangible form. Product claims that are intangible (data per se, software per se) or transitory signals (carrier waves) do not fall within the three product categories. If claim's BRI includes non-statutory embodiments, reject under § 101 and recommend amendment to narrow scope to statutory embodiments. Use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 when appropriate. See MPEP § 2106.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2A — Determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (i.e., a judicial exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial exceptions include abstract ideas (mathematical formulas, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes), laws of nature, natural phenomena, products of nature, scientific principles, and similar concepts. There are no bright-line boundaries; it is sufficient to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception. The examiner should identify the specific claim limitation(s) that may recite the exception. See MPEP § 2106.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2B — Whether the claim recites additional elements amounting to significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), determine whether the claim recites additional elements, either individually or in combination, that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the search for an 'inventive concept' and is assessed by considering whether added limitations transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (practical application). The machine-or-transformation test is an important clue to the 'significantly more' determination but should not be used as a separate test. See MPEP § 2106.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(a) — Improvements to the functioning of a computer or to any other technology or technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that improves an existing technology or the functioning of a computer can supply 'significantly more' and therefore be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consider whether the claim elements provide a technical improvement beyond the judicial exception (examples: Enfish — self‑referential table that improved database technology; McRO — rules of a particular type that improved an existing technological process). If the claim's additional elements are tied to a technological improvement, eligibility is more likely. See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(b) — Particular machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of a particular machine or apparatus (as more than a generic computer) may supply significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims tied to a specific, particular machine (not a generic 'computer') can indicate a practical application of an exception. However, mere recitation of generic computer components (a 'general purpose computer') typically is insufficient (see TLI, In re Alappat history). Examiners should evaluate whether the machine limitation meaningfully limits the claim beyond the judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.05(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(c) — Particular transformation (machine-or-transformation test as a clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed transformation of an article to a different state or thing (particular transformation) can weigh toward 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the machine-or-transformation test is no longer the sole test for eligibility, it remains informative: a claimed transformation of a physical article into a different state or thing tends to indicate eligibility. Examiners should consider whether the claimed process effects a particular transformation. See MPEP § 2106.05(c) and discussion on the test's role as a clue.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(d) — Well-understood, routine, conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the additional claim elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional activities previously known in the field, they typically do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should determine whether the additional elements add anything inventive beyond applying the judicial exception with conventional steps or components. Mere use of routine data gathering, generic computer implementation, or conventional activity will not confer eligibility. See MPEP § 2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(e) — Other meaningful limitations (non-generic arrangement / unconventional combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that supply meaningful constraints — such as unconventional technical solution, non-generic arrangement, or an innovative ordered combination of known elements — may amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify whether the claim recites an unconventional technical solution to a technological problem (example: Amdocs where construction of 'enhance' required distributed field enhancements). A non-generic arrangement of known, conventional elements can change the claim's character. See MPEP § 2106.05(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(f) — Mere instructions to apply an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that simply instruct practitioners to apply an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (e.g., 'apply the formula') do not supply significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that add only generic instructions to implement an exception (e.g., 'apply this mathematical formula') fail to transform the exception into a patent-eligible application. Such 'mere instruction' limitations are insufficient under Step 2B. See MPEP § 2106.05(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(g) — Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim elements that add insignificant post‑solution or ancillary activity (data collection, certain conventional pre/post steps) do not supply significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities that are incidental to the solution of the abstract idea (or that occur after solving it) and that amount to no more than data-gathering, insignificant pre/post-solution steps, or conventional activity should not render the claim eligible. See MPEP § 2106.05(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(h) — Field of use and technological environment limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use, or reciting a technological environment (e.g., 'over the Internet') does not, by itself, make the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An abstract idea does not become nonabstract merely by limiting the invention to a particular field or technological environment. Examiners should look for meaningful limitations beyond a mere field‑of‑use restriction. See MPEP § 2106.05(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Alice/Mayo two-part test is the controlling framework (use only this test for eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court's Alice/Mayo two-part test (identify whether claims are directed to a judicial exception; if so, determine whether additional elements amount to significantly more) is the only test that should be used to evaluate eligibility under examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other tests (e.g., machine-or-transformation) serve as clues for the 'significantly more' inquiry but must be considered within the two-part framework. Examiners should not use superseded tests like 'useful, concrete and tangible result' as the eligibility standard. See MPEP § 2106 summary and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathways A/B/C to eligibility (streamlined analysis vs. full Alice/Mayo analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three pathways to finding eligibility: Pathway A — claims within statutory category with self-evident eligibility (streamlined); Pathway B — claims within statutory category and not directed to judicial exception (Step 2A: NO); Pathway C — claims within statutory category, directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), but recite additional elements amounting to significantly more (Step 2B: YES).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is clearly eligible under Pathway A, a streamlined analysis is appropriate; otherwise, conduct full Step 2A/2B analysis. If unsure whether streamlined analysis applies, perform full analysis. If claim fails all pathways, reject under 35 U.S.C. § 101. See MPEP subsection III and §§ 2106.04–2106.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis — Eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: When eligibility is self-evident from the claim (e.g., claim is clearly within a statutory category and does not implicate any judicial exception), examiner may use a streamlined analysis to find eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should still document rationale. If there is doubt, a full Alice/Mayo analysis is encouraged. See MPEP § 2106.06(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis — Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that clearly improve computer functionality or any other technology can be found eligible under the streamlined pathway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim plainly claims a technological improvement, the examiner may conclude eligibility under streamlined analysis (Pathway A). However, document the specific improvements and supporting specification passages. See MPEP § 2106.06(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify judicial exceptions by examples and labels (no bright lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial exceptions may be described variously (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena, products of nature, mental processes, mathematical algorithms, disembodied concepts). There are no bright lines between types; a concept may fall under more than one label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For analysis it is sufficient to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception and to identify the specific claim limitation(s) implicated. Use case law examples to support the identification. See MPEP § 2106.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern as the underlying consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying concern driving the two-part framework is preemption — preventing monopolization of basic tools of scientific and technological work (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While preemption is not a standalone test, courts examine whether a claim would preempt substantially all uses of the exception; demonstrations of non-preemption (meaningful limitations, particular machines/transformations, improvements) support eligibility. Examiners should consider preemption in Step 2B analysis and cite relevant cases. See MPEP discussion and cited cases (e.g., Mayo, Alice, Ariosa, Rapid Litigation Management).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility analysis should not rely on utility, novelty, or nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-eligibility under § 101 is not determined by utility, novelty (35 U.S.C. 102), or nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. 103); nor by the obsolete 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must use § 101 analysis for eligibility and use §§ 102, 103, 112 to address novelty, obviousness, and written description/enablement issues. Do not conflate § 101 with other patentability requirements. See MPEP discussion referencing cases rejecting reliance on 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' (State Street/In re Alappat history).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating a rejection for lack of subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a § 101 rejection, the examiner must articulate why the claim is directed to a judicial exception and why any added elements do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection should identify the judicial exception and the specific claim limitations implicated, provide a reasoned explanation (including BRI), cite relevant case law and MPEP sections, and, where applicable, use model/form paragraphs. If the claim could be amended to be statutory, recommend amendments. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for procedural guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating applicant's response to a § 101 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant responds (arguments, amendments, evidence), the examiner must evaluate whether the response overcomes the reasoned rejection by addressing directed-to-exception (Step 2A) or showing additional elements amount to significantly more (Step 2B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether proposed amendments meaningfully narrow the claim to statutory embodiments or add limitations that materially change the claim's character. Evaluate new evidence or expert declarations that bear on whether elements are conventional. If response fails, maintain rejection with explanation; if persuasive, withdraw rejection and consider clarifying remarks. See MPEP § 2106.07(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifying the record when issuing eligibility findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may make clarifying remarks on the record whether the claim is found eligible or ineligible to explain rationale, cite specification support, and aid applicant understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When eligible due to an improvement in technology, the examiner can reference parts of the specification and note claim elements that produce the improvement. When issuing a rejection, explaining the BRI and suggesting narrowing amendments aids prosecution. Clarifying remarks may be made at any point during prosecution, including with a notice of allowance. See MPEP § 2106.07(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that encompass both statutory and non-statutory embodiments fail Step 1
rubrics_metrics.description: If the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim covers both statutory embodiments and non-statutory embodiments, the claim as a whole does not fall within a statutory category and fails Step 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases a § 101 rejection should be made for failure to claim statutory subject matter; examiners should point out the BRI and recommend amendments to narrow the claim to statutory embodiments if possible. Example: machine-readable medium claims that encompass carrier waves. See MPEP § 2106.03 and illustrative cases (Mentor Graphics, Nuijten).
